# Epigenetic tuning of PD-1 expression improves exhausted T cell function and viral control

## Abstract

PD-1 is a key negative regulator of CD8+ T cell activation and is highly expressed by exhausted T cells in cancer and chronic viral infection. While PD-1 blockade can improve viral and tumor control, physiologic PD-1 expression prevents immunopathology and improves memory formation. The mechanisms driving high PD-1 expression in exhaustion are not well understood and could be critical to disentangling its beneficial and detrimental effects. Here, we functionally interrogated the epigenetic regulation of PD-1 using a novel mouse model with deletion of an exhaustion-specific PD-1 enhancer. Enhancer deletion exclusively alters PD-1 expression in CD8+ T cells in chronic infection, creating a “sweet spot” of intermediate expression where T cell function is optimized compared to wildtype and PD-1 knockout cells. This permits improved control of chronic infection without additional immunopathology. Together, these results demonstrate that tuning PD-1 via epigenetic editing can reduce CD8+ T cell dysfunction while avoiding excess immunopathology.

## Introduction

T cell exhaustion is a state of CD8+ T cell dysfunction induced in contexts of chronic stimulation such as cancer and chronic viral infection. Compared to functional effector and memory populations, exhausted CD8+ T cells have reduced proliferation and survival, and impaired effector functionality including lower cytotoxicity and cytokine production[1, 2]. Exhausted T cells have distinct transcriptional and epigenetic profiles, and express high levels of multiple inhibitory receptors such as PD-1 and TIM3[3, 4]. This state is regulated by multiple transcription factors including Tox[5–8]. Recent work has defined significant heterogeneity within the exhausted T cell compartment, including a stem-like “progenitor exhausted”, an effector-like “transitory exhausted”, and a most dysfunctional “terminally exhausted” subset[9–13].

The programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) is a critical negative regulator of T cell activation that is upregulated upon activation. With chronic stimulation, exhausted CD8+ T cells exhibit higher, sustained PD-1 expression relative to functional populations such as effector T cells, and this increase in PD-1 signaling reinforces T cell exhaustion[3]. Antibody blockade of PD-1 improves control of chronic viral infection and tumor[3, 14], and this therapeutic strategy is now a cornerstone of treatment for many types of human cancer[15–20]. However, complete loss of PD-1 signaling, such as via genetic knock-out (KO), has both beneficial and detrimental effects on CD8+ T cell fate and function. In mouse models of acute infection such as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) Armstrong and influenza, PD-1 KO cells are defective in memory CD8+ T cell formation, persistence, and re-expansion in response to secondary infection [21, 22]. Furthermore, in a chronic infection model (LCMV Clone 13), PD-1 KO CD8+ T cells proliferate more compared to wildtype (WT) cells early in infection, but become more prone to cell death and exhibit lower cytokine production later in infection[23]. To date, there has been no comprehensive analysis of the mechanisms by which PD-1 is specifically regulated in exhausted T cells.

We previously showed that exhausted CD8+ T cells have a unique chromatin accessibility profile, distinct from naive, effector, and memory populations, and identified an exhaustion-specific open chromatin region (OCR) near the PD-1 gene (Pdcd1) locus[24–26]. To determine the function of this putative enhancer, we used CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing to generate an enhancer-deleted (EnhDel) mouse strain, allowing us to interrogate the impact of this OCR on PD-1 expression and CD8+ T cell state. We found that loss of this region reduces PD-1 expression specifically in chronic, but not acute infection, and increases the persistence of EnhDel compared to WT CD8+ T cells. Critically, EnhDel CD8+ T cells were better able to control chronic viral infection than WT cells without causing the excess immunopathology seen with PD-1 KO cells. These results demonstrate that manipulation of a single enhancer can meaningfully alter T cell function, and that intermediate expression levels permit the development of unique phenotypes.

## Results

### An exhaustion-associated enhancer modulates PD-1 expression

Previous work profiling chromatin accessibility in CD8+ T cells identified an OCR -23kb upstream of the mouse Pdcd1 locus that is accessible in exhausted CD8+ T cells from chronic infection, but not in functional CD8+ T cells from acute infection. This accessibility difference arises between day 3.5 and day 7 and persists to late timepoints (day 28) (Figure 1A). We hypothesized that this region could be responsible for driving the high levels of PD-1 expression associated with greater CD8+ T cell dysfunction in chronic contexts. To this end, we created an enhancer-deleted mouse model, using CRISPR-Cas9 and a pair of guide RNAs to excise the 1.2 kb OCR (Figure 1B). Sanger sequencing confirmed that the entire region was removed without any insertions or deletions at the site of end-joining (Ext. Data Figure 1A).

We compared uninfected EnhDel mice to littermate WT controls to determine the impact of enhancer deletion on immune cell development and PD-1 expression at baseline (Ext. Data Figure 1B). CD8+ T cells were present at a similar frequency within the CD45+ compartment of EnhDel and WT mice in multiple tissues (Figure 1C). This also held true for other immune cell types (CD4+ conventional T cells [Tconv], CD4+ regulatory T cells [Treg], B cells, natural killer [NK] cells, γδ T cells) in the spleen and liver (Ext. Data Figure 1C). EnhDel CD8+ T cells showed no difference in PD-1 expression compared to WT cells (Figure 1C, Ext. Data Figure 1D, E), nor differences in expression of activation/migration markers (Figure 1D, Ext. Data Figure 1F) at baseline. We did note that Treg cells and γδ T cells had lower PD-1 expression in EnhDel mice (Ext. Data Figure 1D, Treg: p = 0.0005, γδ T: p = 0.002), consistent with published ATAC-seq tracks[27] showing OCR accessibility in these populations (Ext. Data Figure 1G). Interestingly, Treg cells and γδ T cells had the highest level of PD-1 expression at baseline, by flow cytometry as well as in published transcriptional profiling[27]. These data suggest that this enhancer may be used by immune cells specifically to sustain PD-1 expression.

As PD-1 is transiently upregulated with T cell activation, we next asked whether EnhDel CD8+ T cells differ from WT cells in response to acute in vitro stimulation. After 72 hours of stimulation with anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies (Figure 1E), EnhDel cells upregulated PD-1 to similar levels as WT cells, by percentage and magnitude (geometric mean fluorescence intensity, gMFI) (Figure 1F). There was also no difference in proliferation by CTV dilution (Ext. Data Figure 1H), further supporting that enhancer deletion does not globally alter PD-1 regulation in CD8+ T cells.

We next investigated how enhancer deletion affects PD-1 expression in vivo during viral infection, hypothesizing that enhancer deletion would decrease PD-1 expression in chronic but not acute LCMV infection. To identify cell-intrinsic differences between EnhDel and WT cells while controlling for TCR specificity and environmental milieu, we bred the EnhDel strain onto the LCMV-specific P14 TCR-transgenic background, then co-transferred congenically-marked EnhDel and WT P14+ CD8+ T cells into WT recipients (Figure 1G). Recipients were infected with LCMV Clone 13 (Cl. 13) with CD4 depletion (Ext. Data Figure 2A) or LCMV Armstrong (Arm.), and transferred cells were recovered from the spleen and profiled at early (days 7–8) as well as late (days 28–30) timepoints (Ext. Data Figure 2B, Figure 1H). We used littermate donor mice for all competitive transfer experiments to control for possible off-target effects of CRISPR editing. We optimized a low-dose transfer of 1500 cells to permit adequate cell recovery without perturbing infection chronicity[28], and confirmed with viral titer (Ext. Data Figure 2C). A similar percentage of co-transferred EnhDel and WT P14+ cells expressed PD-1 both early and late in Arm. infection. In contrast, a lower percentage of EnhDel cells expressed PD-1 late in Cl. 13 infection (p = 0.002) (Figure 1I). We examined differences in the magnitude of expression between EnhDel and WT cells by calculating the relative gMFI within the PD-1-positive compartment, which allowed us to compare across timepoints and contexts. During both in vitro stimulation and Arm. infection, EnhDel and WT cells expressed similar levels of PD-1, with an average gMFI ratio (EnhDel/WT) close to 1. In contrast, EnhDel cells isolated from Cl. 13 infection had an approximately 50% lower PD-1 gMFI relative to WT cells, which was significantly different from Arm. at both early (p = 4E-18) and late (p = 9E-18) timepoints (Figure 1H, 1J). Thus, enhancer deletion decreases PD-1 expression specifically in chronic infection while preserving expression in other settings of T cell activation.

### Enhancer deletion expands CD8+ T cells in chronic infection

We next asked whether the enhancer deletion-mediated reduction in PD-1 expression was sufficient to alter aspects of CD8+ T cell function, including T cell expansion, persistence, and differentiation. We utilized our P14+ co-transfer model (Figure 1G) to compare the numbers of EnhDel versus WT CD8+ T cells over time. At day 28–30 of chronic infection, we found significantly more EnhDel than WT cells (p = 7.2E-5, Figure 2A). This numerical advantage was specific to chronic infection and not seen in acute infection (p = 8.2E-5, Figure 2B). EnhDel cells had a numerical advantage as early as day 7 (p = 0.01), and this lasted beyond day 50 (p = 0.001, Figure 2C). In acute infection, contrastingly, EnhDel cell numbers remained similar to WT from an effector-predominant early timepoint to memory-predominant late timepoints (Figure 2C).

As there is substantial heterogeneity within the exhausted compartment, we next examined the impact of enhancer deletion on subset formation. We defined the progenitor exhausted subset (prog.) by expression of Slamf6 and lack of TIM3 expression; we subdivided TIM3 expressing cells into effector-like exhausted (eff.-like, CX3CR1-positive) and terminally exhausted (term., CX3CR1-negative) (Figure 2D)[10, 11]. Enhancer deletion conferred a reduction in the level of PD-1 across subsets at both early (p < 1.8E-17) and late (p < 5.0E-6) timepoints (Figure 2E), suggesting that this enhancer globally regulates PD-1 in exhaustion. This was associated with differences in subset distribution across the infection timecourse. At day 7, EnhDel cells were biased toward the prog. subset (p = 9.3E-6) and the term. subset (p = 2.4E-6) (Ext. Data Figure 2D), whereas at day 30, only the term. subset was enriched in EnhDel cells (p = 0.049), while the prog. and eff.-like subsets were enriched in WT cells (p = 0.001 and p = 0.049) (Figure 2F).

To further contextualize the effects of reduced PD-1 expression via enhancer deletion, we examined the impact of further reducing PD-1 signaling through blockade of its ligand, PD-L1. Utilizing our co-transfer system, we treated LCMV Cl. 13-infected co-transfer recipients with anti-PD-L1 blocking antibody on days 15, 18, 21, 24, and 27 of infection[12], then analyzed transferred cell phenotype on day 30 (Ext. Data Figure 2E). Both WT and EnhDel cells expanded in response to PD-1 pathway blockade (EnhDel: p = 0.039, WT: p = 0.0027) (Ext. Data Figure 2F). This was associated with a bias away from the prog. subset (EnhDel: p = 0.024, WT: p = 0.0023), and towards the term. state (EnhDel: p = 0.030, WT: p = 0.0015) in both genotypes (Ext. Data Figure 2G). Interestingly, EnhDel cells maintained their numerical advantage over WT cells with anti-PD-L1 treatment (aPD-L1: p = 0.0026, control: p = 0.00097) (Ext. Data Figure 2F). This demonstrates that EnhDel cells remain responsive to additional PD-1 pathway manipulation, and that the early EnhDel numerical advantage persists through additional expansion via PD-L1 blockade.

### Enhancer deletion augments cell proliferation and survival

We next investigated the mechanisms underlying the EnhDel numerical advantage. As complete loss of PD-1 via gene knockout impacts both T cell proliferation and apoptosis during chronic infection[23], we interrogated the effect of enhancer deletion on both processes. We assayed proliferation using BrdU incorporation (Figure 3A, Ext. Data Figure 2H) and found that EnhDel cells were more proliferative than WT cells, particularly at earlier timepoints (day 7, day 15). This was true both within the total CD8+ T cell compartment at D7 (p = 0.007) and D15 (p = 0.01) (Ext. Data Figure 2I) as well as within less differentiated subsets (D7 prog. p = 0.01, D7 eff.-like p = 0.0001; D15 prog. p = 4.0E-5, D15 eff.-like p = 0.001) (Figure 3B). In addition, EnhDel cells were less apoptotic as measured by Annexin V staining (Figure 3C, Ext. Data Figure 2J), in marked contrast to the PD-1 KO phenotype[23]. This apoptosis-reduction was observed at D15 (p = 0.002) and D29 (p = 0.0001), both within the total CD8+ T cell compartment (Ext. Data Figure 2K) and within more differentiated subsets (D15 term. p = 0.0005; D29 eff.-like p = 0.02, D29 term. p = 3.4E-5) (Figure 3D). Since the impact of enhancer deletion on proliferation and cell death varied with subset and timepoint, we wondered if this could be related to relative differences in PD-1 expression by exhausted subsets over time[29]. Indeed, in both EnhDel and WT cells, PD-1 expression was higher in the prog. compared to term. subset early, but higher in the term. subset late in infection (Ext. Data Figure 2L, Ext. Data Figure 2M). This suggests a model in which the effects of enhancer deletion on proliferation and apoptosis predominate in the exhausted subset expressing the highest levels of PD-1 at a given timepoint. Together, these data demonstrate that the intact exhaustion-associated PD-1 enhancer restrains early proliferation in progenitor-exhausted cells and promotes late cell death in terminally-exhausted cells.

### PD-1 perturbation does not generate novel exhausted subsets

As enhancer deletion modulates both proliferation and cell death, we next investigated the effects of reduced PD-1 expression on the broader exhausted CD8+ T cell state. We transcriptionally profiled exhausted CD8+ T cells with three distinct levels of PD-1 expression: WT cells with unaltered expression, EnhDel cells with reduced expression, and PD-1 KO cells with absent expression. We co-transferred cells of all three genotypes (P14+ EnhDel, WT, and PD-1 KO) into GFP-expressing recipient mice, followed by Cl. 13 infection (Figure 4A). On day 30 of infection, transferred cells were sorted by absent GFP expression and by genotype via CD45 congenic expression (Figure 4B). We then performed scRNA-seq to capture the full heterogeneity of differentiation states within these three genotypes. All samples showed similar distributions of quality metrics after preliminary filtering (Ext. Data Figure 3A), and 27,632 cells underwent further analysis.

We first examined whether genetic perturbation of PD-1 expression (by gene knockout or enhancer deletion) impacted the formation and distribution of exhausted CD8+ T cells across scRNA-seq clusters. UMAP projection and Louvain clustering revealed five main subpopulations (Figure 4C), without any defined by a single sample (Ext. Data Figure 3B). All clusters showed strong Tox expression, confirming T cell exhaustion in all genotypes. Exhausted subset-specific markers (Slamf6, Havcr2, Cx3cr1, Cd101, Mki67) identified progenitor, effector-like, transitory, terminal, and dividing clusters (Figure 4D, Ext. Data Figure 3C). To confirm these annotations, we generated subset-specific signatures from bulk RNA-seq data[10] to score each cluster. As expected, the progenitor and terminal signatures enriched in their corresponding clusters, and the transitory-exhausted signature enriched in the remaining three clusters (Ext. Data Figure 3D).

We next determined the distribution of genotypes across the clusters. In the UMAP, WT and PD-1 KO cells were largely non-overlapping: WT cells enriched in the eff.-like cluster, while PD-1 KO cells enriched in the term. cluster (Figure 4E). EnhDel cells occupied an intermediate profile, with substantial density in all clusters. To quantitate these genotype-specific cluster biases, we calculated the percentage of each cluster derived from each genotype, normalizing for differences in total cell number per genotype (Figure 4F). Compared to both EnhDel and WT, PD-1 KO cells were enriched in the terminal cluster and depleted in all others (all p < 4.4E-5). In contrast, EnhDel and WT cells had a similar cluster distribution, only differing significantly in the eff.-like and term. clusters (p < 1.2E-30).

As exhausted subsets are defined by key epigenetic as well as transcriptional differences[25, 30], we next asked whether genetically modulating PD-1 expression could alter the epigenetic regulation of exhausted T cells. We compared chromatin accessibility profiles by co-transferring EnhDel with WT cells, or EnhDel with PD-1 KO cells, followed by Cl. 13 infection (Figure 4G). At day 30, we sorted transferred cells by genotype and exhausted subset (progenitor: Slamf6+ TIM3−, terminal: Slamf6− TIM3+ CX3CR1−) for ATAC-seq. Data quality was verified with robust accessibility near transcription start sites (TSS) (Ext. Data Figure 3E) and replicate correlation (Ext. Data Figure 3F). Additionally, the expected -23.8kb OCR at the PD-1 locus was present in WT and PD-1 KO samples, but completely absent in the EnhDel samples (Figure 4H). Assessing similarity between conditions with the Spearman correlation coefficient revealed that all three genotypes clustered together by subset, with prog. T cells particularly tightly correlated across genotypes (Figure 4I). To quantify the degree of genotype-specific differences within subset, we identified differentially accessible peaks between genotypes (EnhDel versus PD-1 KO, EnhDel versus WT, and PD-1 KO versus WT) for each exhausted subset. Across all comparisons, there were very few differences, with non-differential peaks comprising 94.74% or more of each relevant peak universe (Figure 4J).

Leveraging our ATAC-seq data, we next interrogated the putative transcription factors binding to the exhaustion-associated Pdcd1 enhancer. We utilized the TOBIAS computational suite[31] to assign footprinting scores and estimate occupancy for all vertebrate motifs in the JASPAR database[32]. 148 transcription factors were predicted to be bound within the enhancer, with the substantial majority (85.8%) predicted in both exhausted subsets (Ext. Data Figure 3G). This included many exhaustion-associated transcription factors (Nr4a2, Rara, Runx3, Stat5a), including one (Nr4a1) with ChIP-qPCR-validated binding at the predicted site within the enhancer[33]. Most of the subset-specific binding predictions were in the prog.-exhausted subset (20 motifs). These transcription factors were also more highly expressed in prog.-exhausted cells in our scRNA-seq data (Ext. Data Figure 3H), consistent with higher expression contributing to greater binding. More broadly, however, our footprinting analysis suggests that the exhaustion-associated Pdcd1 enhancer operates similarly across exhausted subsets.

Taken together, our scRNA-seq and ATAC-seq analyses demonstrate that neither enhancer deletion nor PD-1 knock-out fundamentally alter the formation of exhausted T cell subsets: all genotypes contribute cells to all scRNA-seq clusters, and the chromatin accessibility profiles of both profiled subsets are overwhelmingly similar across genotypes.

### Enhancer deletion uniquely induces an effector gene program

Given that the examined genotypes differed in scRNA-seq cluster distribution, we next asked whether genetic perturbation of PD-1 could alter transcriptional state within a cluster. We began by utilizing principal component analysis (PCA) to identify the strongest axes of variation and the strongest gene contributions to variation between genotypes. Per cluster, we averaged the gene expression of all cells of a given sample (genotype/replicate) to create a “pseudo-bulk” RNA-seq profile, then performed PCA on the resulting samples (Figure 5A). Across all clusters, principal component 1 (PC1) placed WT and PD-1 KO samples on either extreme with EnhDel samples in an intermediate position. Genes that were most PD-1 KO-associated, or positively-weighted in PC1, included canonical exhaustion genes such as Tox, Nr4a2, Ctla4, Cd244, Ikzf2, as well as terminal-exhaustion-associated genes Cd7 and Car2 (Ext. Data Figure 4A–C)[5–8, 10, 33, 34]. The second axis of variation (PC2), in contrast, uniquely separated the EnhDel samples from both WT and PD-1 KO. EnhDel-associated genes (positively-weighted in PC2) included effector-associated genes such as Klrg1, Gzmb, Lgals1, and Lgals3[5] and multiple NK-associated KLR genes (Klre1, Klrk1, Klrd1) (Figure 5B).

In addition to comparing our genotypes at the individual gene level, we used gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)[35, 36] to understand distinguishing biological patterns between genotypes. Within each cluster, we generated a differential gene list for each genotype comparison (EnhDel versus WT, EnhDel versus PD-1 KO, PD-1 KO versus WT) and examined the enrichment of canonical pathways and immunologic gene sets. To identify unique aspects of EnhDel biology, we focused on gene sets that were consistently enriched or depleted in both EnhDel comparisons (versus PD-1 KO and versus WT) and in multiple clusters (Figure 5C–D). EnhDel-enriched gene sets included several related to the effector state (Figure 5E), and to oxidative phosphorylation and the electron transport chain (Figure 5F). Furthermore, consistent with our flow phenotyping, an apoptosis-related signature was depleted in EnhDel compared to WT cells, and notably compared to PD-1 KO cells as well (Ext. Data Figure 4D). Together, these analyses suggest that the transcriptional profile of PD-1 KO cells is more deeply exhausted than EnhDel and WT cells. While EnhDel cells occupy an intermediate state for certain transcriptional features, multiple effector-associated genes and pathways uniquely enrich in EnhDel cells relative to both PD-1 KO and WT cells.

We further leveraged our scRNA-Seq data to evaluate potential off-target effects of CRISPR editing on EnhDel cells. We utilized the CRISPick tool (broad.io/crispick) to predict potential off-target sites for the two sgRNAs utilized in enhancer deletion (Ext. Data Figure 1A). We selected genes with a >30% predicted probability of an off-target cut and compared EnhDel and WT expression patterns. We hypothesized that a productive edit would result in lower expression; however, none of the genes examined showed consistent differential expression between EnhDel and WT cells (Ext. Data Figure 4E). This validates that the on-target impact on PD-1 expression, and not off-target editing, underlies the EnhDel phenotype.

While we focused our primary transcriptional and epigenetic analyses on late chronic infection, a gold-standard context for exhaustion, our flow cytometry data demonstrate that enhancer deletion also affects CD8+ T cells at early timepoints. To interrogate if EnhDel-associated differences change over the course of infection, we profiled co-transferred EnhDel and WT P14+ CD8+ T cells, sorted by subset (prog.: Slamf6+TIM3−, term.: Slamf6−TIM3+CX3CR1−), at day 9 of chronic infection with bulk RNA-Seq. We again used GSEA to identify key biological patterns that differ between EnhDel and WT cells. We found that the differential gene sets identified at day 9 overlap significantly with those from day 30 (Fisher’s Exact, p < 2.2E-16 for both subsets) (Ext. Data Figure 4F), and include key signatures such as oxidative phosphorylation and effector vs. exhausted (Ext. Data Figure 4G–H). This suggests that the transcriptional effects of enhancer deletion are largely consistent over the course of chronic infection. Differences in EnhDel phenotype over time (as with proliferation and apoptosis) may arise from interactions between enhancer-affected gene programs and timepoint-associated gene programs.

### Both intermediate and unique function seen in EnhDel cells

To validate the genotype-specific differences highlighted by our genomic analyses, we assessed the function of co-transferred EnhDel and PD-1 KO CD8+ T cells, as well as co-transferred EnhDel and WT CD8+ T cells, in chronic infection (Figure 6A, Ext. Data Figure 5A). At day 28–30, PD-1 KO cells had a numerical advantage over EnhDel cells (p = 1.1E-12) (Figure 6B) but were strongly biased towards the terminal subset (p = 1.8E-6) (Figure 6C, Ext. Data Figure 5B). This is consistent with our scRNA-seq analysis demonstrating PD-1 KO cells enriched in the terminally-exhausted cluster.

As EnhDel cells uniquely enriched for an effector-versus-exhausted gene signature[5] by scRNA-seq, we investigated cytokine production and cytotoxic potential as two key aspects of effector function. We first examined IFNγ and TNF expression following ex vivo gp33 peptide re-stimulation. PD-1 KO cells expressed less IFNγ compared to EnhDel cells, particularly in the prog. (p = 2.5E-5) and term. (p = 0.0003) subsets (Figure 6D). EnhDel cells expressed less IFNγ than WT cells; as with the EnhDel/PD-1 KO comparison, this difference was significant in the prog. (p = 3.3E-6) and term. (p = 0.005) subsets. No significant differences were observed in TNF production across genotypes and subsets (Ext. Data Figure 5C–5D). With respect to cytotoxic potential, PD-1 KO cells expressed more Granzyme B (Gzmb) than EnhDel cells in the prog. subset (p = 0.006), but EnhDel cells were more Gzmb+ than PD-1 KO cells in the eff.-like (p = 0.0003) and term. (p = 8.8E-8) subsets (Figure 6E). Interestingly, EnhDel cells expressed comparable levels of Gzmb compared to WT cells across subsets, in contrast to the corresponding IFNγ comparison.

Next, we measured expression of KLRG1 and Tox as markers of effector and exhausted states, respectively. Strikingly, Tox expression was lower in EnhDel cells compared to both PD-1 KO (p < 3.0E-5, all subsets) and WT cells (p < 0.02, all subsets) (Figure 6F). Following a similar pattern, KLRG1 expression was higher in EnhDel cells compared to both PD-1 KO and WT cells in the eff.-like subset, as well as in the term. subset compared to PD-1 KO cells (p < 0.006 in all highlighted comparisons) (Figure 6G, Ext. Data Figure 5E). Lastly, EnhDel cells had lower levels of Annexin V staining in the eff.-like and term. populations, compared to both PD-1 KO (p = 0.0001 and p = 0.0004, respectively) and WT cells (p = 0.02 and p = 3.4E-5, respectively) (Figure 6H, Ext. Data Figure 5F); this was again consistent with our scRNA-seq GSEA results.

These comparisons demonstrate that an intermediate level of PD-1 expression can modulate the exhaustion phenotype in multiple ways. For some aspects (numerical advantage, IFNγ production), intermediate PD-1 expression via enhancer deletion creates an intermediate phenotype between complete loss (PD-1 KO) and WT expression. For other features (granzyme B), reduced PD-1 expression does not alter the WT phenotype, while complete loss of PD-1 does. Finally, intermediate PD-1 expression leads to certain unique benefits compared to both WT and absent PD-1 expression, including increased KLRG1, decreased Tox, and decreased apoptosis.

### EnhDel cells improve viral control with limited host damage

Lastly, we investigated the impact of enhancer deletion on disease progression and host health. Complete lack of PD-1, whether in all cells or in transferred CD8+ T cells, improves viral control but also leads to immune-mediated tissue damage and fatal circulatory collapse[3, 23, 37]. We hypothesized that an EnhDel cell transfer would lead to improved viral control relative to WT cells, while ameliorating the fatal pathology associated with PD-1 KO cells. To this end, we transferred either WT, EnhDel, or PD-1 KO P14 cells into recipient animals and infected them with LCMV Cl. 13 (Figure 7A). We monitored for weight loss and death, and assayed serum and spleen at an early (day 7) and chronic (day 30) timepoint.

Recipients of an EnhDel transfer lost less weight compared to mice that either received a WT or PD-1 KO transfer, particularly at the point of maximum weight loss (p < 0.002 at day 12, both comparisons) (Figure 7B). Analysis of recipient animal survival (Figure 7C) confirmed that PD-1 KO cell recipients survived less well than WT cell recipients (p = 0.021), as expected. In contrast, EnhDel cell recipients survived comparably to WT cell recipients (p = 0.993) and had better survival than PD-1 KO cell recipients (p = 0.024).

To further interrogate the reduced weight loss phenotype with EnhDel transfer, we examined metrics of inflammation, cell phenotype, and viral titer at an early timepoint. In serum cytokine analysis from day 7 (Ext. Data Figure 6A–B), EnhDel transfer recipients had lower levels of IFNγ (p = 0.028) and TNF (p = 0.007), and comparable levels of IL-6 (p = 0.65), compared to WT transfer recipients (Figure 7D). This is in direct contrast to published PD-1 KO-mediated increases in serum cytokines (IFNγ, TNF, and IL-6)[37]. At this early timepoint, mice receiving EnhDel cells had more transferred cells (p = 0.044) (Figure 7E) and significantly lower serum viral titers (p = 0.026) (Figure 7F) compared to WT transfer recipients. These data suggest that enhancer deletion prevents excessive weight loss due to lower viral titers in early infection and less consequent viral-mediated inflammation and damage.

Furthermore, the effects of EnhDel transfer were sustained to a chronic timepoint (day 30) of LCMV Cl. 13. EnhDel transferred cells were recovered at higher numbers than WT cells from recipient spleens on D30 of infection (Figure 7G, p = 0.0037), and a transfer of EnhDel cells was sufficient to improve viral control compared to a WT transfer (Figure 7H, p = 0.0036). Across multiple timepoints, our results demonstrate that enhancer deletion is sufficient to meaningfully improve exhausted CD8+ T cell functionality, without the imbalance between host defense and host damage seen with complete loss of PD-1 signaling.

## Discussion

The co-inhibitory receptor PD-1 plays a key role in regulating CD8+ T cell exhaustion. While gene knockout of PD-1 expands exhausted cell numbers, it also leads to deeper functional deficits and poorer cell survival. To investigate whether an intermediate level of PD-1 expression could confer an improved balance of exhausted CD8+ T cell functionality, we created a novel mouse model in which an exhaustion-specific enhancer of PD-1 was deleted. We find that the effects of enhancer deletion are strictly focused to specific cell states: PD-1 expression by EnhDel CD8+ T cells differs from WT CD8+ cells in exhaustion but is indistinguishable in other contexts. Lowering PD-1 expression through enhancer deletion both increases proliferation and decreases apoptosis, leading to a greater number of EnhDel exhausted cells. While PD-1 KO CD8+ T cells are strongly biased towards terminal exhaustion, EnhDel cells enrich for effector-associated gene signatures. We identified several key phenotypes unique to EnhDel CD8+ T cells compared to both WT and PD-1 KO cells, including lower expression of the exhaustion-associated transcription factor Tox. Finally, we demonstrated that EnhDel-associated functional changes are sufficient to improve viral control in chronic infection, without leading to PD-1 KO-associated immunopathology.

Our study has several important implications for understanding PD-1 regulation, exhausted CD8+ T cell biology, and enhancer editing. First, our results demonstrate that enhancer editing can target the effects of a genetic perturbation to a specific context. The cell states, and cell types, with enhancer accessibility exhibited reduced PD-1 expression with enhancer deletion, while no effect was seen where the enhancer was closed. This pattern extended to additional phenotypic aspects, including unaltered CD8+ T cell numbers and activation state at baseline, unaltered expansion following in vitro stimulation, and unaltered memory T cell formation after acute infection. This differentiates enhancer deletion from PD-1 KO, which has been shown to negatively impact memory formation and recall responses[21, 22]. Further work is needed to interrogate the consequences of enhancer deletion in other enhancer-accessible compartments, including Treg cells and γδ T cells.

Second, we have demonstrated that an intermediate level of PD-1 expression leads to certain “sweet spot” properties, for which intermediate expression is uniquely beneficial compared to both wildtype and absent expression. Complete loss of PD-1 signaling in PD-1 KO cells leads to an increase in other negative regulatory mechanisms, including upregulation of exhaustion-associated genes like Ctla4 and Cd160. Enhancer deletion may prevent these compensatory changes through more subtle tuning of PD-1 signaling and downstream TCR/CD28 signaling. A similar pattern is seen with Tox, in which complete loss of Tox leads to absent exhausted cell persistence, while reduced Tox expression confers enhanced tumor control[7]. These data suggest that the “sweet spot” concept may apply more generally to key regulators of exhaustion biology. Our results also highlight the complexity of PD-1-mediated regulation: the processes regulated by PD-1 vary by exhausted subset and timepoint, as seen with proliferation and apoptosis in EnhDel versus WT cells. Dissecting how specific functions are differentially impacted would deepen our understanding of PD-1 signaling, and could suggest additional targets to optimize the effects of PD-1 modulation on exhausted CD8+ T cell number and functionality.

Finally, our enhancer editing may represent a proof-of-concept for engineering adoptive cell therapies like CAR-T. Knockout of PD-1 in this context is already moving towards the clinic[38–40]. However, there is early evidence that complete PD-1 loss may lead to reduced CAR-T persistence[38, 41], as has been observed with PD-1 KO CD8+ T cells in mouse chronic infection. Strategies like enhancer editing could provide a way to balance the benefits and liabilities of reduced PD-1 signaling. Furthermore, while PD-1 is one key regulator of the exhausted CD8+ T cell state, there are many additional critical genes with exhaustion-specific chromatin accessible regions. Deletion of these regions, alone or in combination, may reveal approaches to improve and sustain CD8+ T cell effector function in contexts of exhaustion.

## Methods

### Mice

Recipient female C75BL/6J mice and GFP+ mice (C57BL/6-Tg(UBC-GFP)30Scha/J) were purchased (The Jackson Laboratory) at 5 weeks of age and used at 6–7 weeks of age. Breeding pairs of enhancer-deleted mice (B6- Pdcd1tm23kbenhWnh/J) are readily available from the corresponding authors upon request; all other strains can be obtained from The Jackson Laboratory.

All mice were housed in specific pathogen-free conditions with a 12-hour light cycle and a 12-hour dark cycle, 30–70% relative humidity, and 21.1°C ambient temperature. All experiments followed the animal care guidelines from the Harvard Medical School Standing Committee on Animals and the National Institutes of Health (Protocol number: IS00000041–6).

### Enhancer-deleted mouse generation, deletion sequencing, and baseline characterization

To generate enhancer-deleted mice, in vitro transcribed guides targeting upstream (GGACATCTGGAGTCCACAGA) and downstream (GATTAGCCCGAGACAGGCTA) of the enhancer were injected into P14 (B6.Cg-Tg(TcrLCMV)327Sdz) fertilized eggs with Cas9 mRNA. Offspring were analyzed by PCR as well as Sanger sequencing of the predicted deletion.

The PCR genotyping strategy consisted of one FWD primer (sequence: ACAGTTTCATCTGTTCAGGTCAG) and two REV primers: one within the deleted region (only amplified in WT, sequence: CTCAAAGCCGTCTGTGGACT) and one downstream of the deleted region (too distant for efficient amplification in WT, thus only amplified in EnhDel mice, sequence: AGGAACCGACTGGTAGGGATA), to allow identification of EnhDel mice, heterozygotes, and WT mice. For Sanger sequencing, the following primers were used: FWD:

ACAGTTTCATCTGTTCAGGTCAG, REV: AGGAACCGACTGGTAGGGATA. Sanger sequencing was performed by Genewiz Inc (Azenta Life Sciences).

One founder was identified and bred successfully. Enhancer-deleted mice were backcrossed for five generations to C57/BL6J mice, as well as crossed to CD45.1 (B6.SJL-Ptprca Pepcb/BoyJ) and PD-1 KO (B6.Cg-Pdcd1tm1.1Shr/J) strains purchased from The Jackson Laboratory.

Enhancer-deleted and littermate WT mice ages 7–13 weeks were utilized for baseline characterization. Spleen, liver, thymus, bone marrow, and inguinal lymph node were dissected, mechanically dissociated, and filtered to single cell suspension. Leukocytes were enriched from liver tissue using an Optiprep (Sigma) density gradient. Cells were processed for flow cytometry as described below.

For in vitro stimulation, 96-well U-bottomed plates were coated with 1 μg/mL anti-CD3 (Fisher Scientific) and 1 μg/mL anti-CD28 (Fisher Scientific) overnight at 4°C. T cells were isolated using the Pan T Cell Isolation Kit II for mouse (Miltenyi Biotec), and labeled with 0.5 μM CellTrace Violet (ThermoFisher Scientific) for 8 min at 37°C. 50,000 cells per well were plated in RPMI-10 with 100 U/mL recombinant human IL-2 (PeproTech). Cells were harvested after 72 hours and processed for flow cytometry as described below.

### In vivo transfers and LCMV viral infections

All donors were genotyped at Transnetyx for enhancer deletion, PD-1 knockout, P14 allele, and CD45 congenic. Paired (EnhDel and WT, or EnhDel and PD-1 KO) co-transfer and single-transfer donors were selected from within a mouse strain (P14 EnhDel or P14 EnhDel PD-1 KO). Paired donors were typically littermates, were 8–15 weeks old with no more than two weeks of difference in age.

For co-transfer experiments, paired donors were selected to be distinguishable by CD45 congenic markers. Spleens were harvested from donor mice, filtered to a single cell suspension, and enriched for CD8+ T cells using the CD8a+ T cell Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec). Cells were counted and mixed to achieve a 50–50 ratio. Expression of P14, CD45 congenics, and mix ratio were confirmed by flow cytometry prior to transfer. Cells were diluted in RPMI with 1% FBS, and 1500 cells in 200 μL were transferred by intravenous injection into recipient animals the day prior to infection.

For single-transfer experiments, cells were isolated as described above. After counting, all three genotypes were separately resuspended at 1E6 cells per mL. Aliquots of each genotype were stained with CD45.1 or CD45.2 with a unique fluorophore (PE, APC or FITC), then equal volumes of each genotype were mixed and analyzed by flow cytometry to confirm consistent cell concentrations across genotypes. Unstained cells were then diluted in RPMI with 1% FBS, and 2.5E4 cells in 200 μL were transferred by intravenous injection into recipient animals the day prior to infection.

For LCMV Clone 13 infection, mice were treated with 200 μg anti-CD4 depleting antibody (clone GK1.5, BioXcell) on days prior to and following infection (D-1, D1). Mice were infected with 4E6 pfu of LCMV Clone 13 diluted in RPMI + 1% FBS by intravenous injection.

For LCMV Armstrong infection, mice were infected with 2E5 pfu of LCMV Armstrong diluted in RPMI + 1% FBS by intraperitoneal injection.

Mice were weighed every three days after infection. Viral titers were assayed by plaque assay[42]. Blood was collected by cardiac puncture and serum was isolated using Gold Serum Separator Tubes (BD), then frozen at -80°C. Thawed diluted serum was plated on Vero cells (gift from the Wherry lab). Cells were covered with a 50–50 mixture of 2x 199 media (ThermoFisher Scientific) and 1% low-melt temperature agarose (Invitrogen) and allowed to form plaques over 84 hours. Agarose was removed, cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Electron Microscopy Sciences) for 10 minutes at room temperature, and stained with 0.5% crystal violet (Sigma-Aldrich) in a 20% ethanol solution.

### PD-1 pathway blockade

After LCMV Clone 13 infection and EnhDel/WT co-transfer as described above, mice were treated with anti-PD-L1 (200μg per injection, 10F.9G2, BioXCell) or isotype control (Rat IgG2b, κ) antibody on days 15, 18, 21, 24, and 27 of infection. On day 30, spleens were harvested and processed as below.

### CD8+ T cell isolation, flow cytometry, cytokine production, Cytokine Bead Array assay

On the indicated days after LCMV infection, spleens were dissected and filtered to a single-cell suspension. CD8+ T cells were enriched using a CD8a+ T cell isolation kit (Miltenyi) and filtrated to single-cell suspension.

For intracellular assessment of cytokine production, 25% of spleen samples (approx. 10E6 to 25E6 cells) were plated in RPMI + 10% FBS in a 24 well plate with GP33–41 peptide (1:10,000 dilution, NIH Tetramer Core Facility), GolgiStop (1:250 dilution, BD Biosciences), and GolgiPlug (1:500 dilution, BD Biosciences) for 5 hours at 37°C.

For extracellular staining, cells were blocked with 2% anti-mouse CD16/32 (Biolegend) and surface stained with the indicated antibodies (Supplementary Table 4, 1:100 dilution) and Live/Dead Fixable Near-IR dye (1:1000 dilution, Invitrogen) for 25 min at 4°C. Samples were washed with PBS + 2% FBS + 4mM EDTA and spun at 400g for 5 minutes.

For staining of Granzyme B or Tox, cells were fixed with the eBioscience Intracellular Fixation & Permeabilization Buffer Set (ThermoFisher Scientific). For FoxP3 staining, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the eBioscience Foxp3/Transcription Factor Staining Buffer Set (Invitrogen). Following fixation, samples were stained with intracellular antibodies at 1:50 at room temperature for 20 minutes. Samples were washed with the appropriate kit buffer and spun at 500g for 5 minutes.

For cytokine staining, cells were fixed with the Cytofix/Cytoperm Fixation/Permeabilization Solution Kit (BD). Samples were blocked with 5% mouse and 5% rat serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch) and 1% anti-mouse CD16/32, then stained with intracellular antibodies at 1:50. For BrdU experiments, mice were administered 1 mg BrdU (BD Pharmingen) via intraperitoneal injection 14–16 hours prior to tissue harvest. BrdU staining was performed after cell surface staining as per BrdU kit protocol. For Annexin V staining, cell surface staining was performed first as described above. Cells were washed with PBS 2x prior to resuspension in 100 μL of Annexin V binding buffer with Annexin V-PE stain at 1:100 (ThermoFisher). Cells were stained at room temperature for 15 minutes prior to addition of 400 μL Annexin V binding buffer.

AccuCount Fluorescent particles (Spherotech) were added for cell quantification before analysis on an LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences). Data were collected using FACSDiva (v.8.0.1, BD Pharmingen). Analysis was performed using FlowJo (v10.8.0, TreeStar) using fluorescence-minus-one thresholds to set gate margins when appropriate.

Serum cytokine levels were assessed using the Cytometric Bead Array Mouse Inflammation Kit (BD) per manufacturer’s instruction. Briefly, standards were diluted to range from 5 pg/mL to 5000 pg/mL. Samples and standards were combined with beads and detection reagent at a 1:1:1 ratio (20 μL per component). After incubation for 2 hours at room temperature, samples were collected on an Accuri C6 (BD), with analysis in FlowJo as above.

### Single-cell RNA-seq library preparation and analysis

Donor cells were isolated and mixed as described above, at a ⅓:⅓:⅓ ratio (EnhDel:WT:PD-1 KO) for a total transfer dose of 1500 cells per recipient (C57BL/6-Tg(UBC-GFP)30Scha/J, from The Jackson Laboratory). Cell transfer and LCMV Clone 13 infection were performed as above, except without utilizing anti-CD4 antibody. CD8+ T cells were isolated from spleen as described above on D27 post-infection.

Cells were pooled into two samples (sample 1: 2 mice, sample 2: 3 mice). The following populations were then sorted on a FACS Aria II (BD Biosciences): (1) live CD8b+ CD44+ GFP− CD45.1+, (2) live CD8b+ CD44+ GFP− CD45.1+ CD45.2+, (3) live CD8b+ CD44+ GFP− CD45.2+. Cells were counted and loaded onto the Chromium Controller (10X Genomics) for a target recovery of 6,000 single cells per sample. Samples were processed using the 10X Single Cell 3’v3 kit per manufacturer’s protocol. Sequencing was done on an Illumina NextSeq 500 sequencer using a 75-bp kit with paired-end reads.

The Cell Ranger analysis pipeline (v.3.1.0) performed sample demultiplexing, barcode processing, alignment, filtering, UMI counting, and aggregation of sequencing runs. Transcripts were aligned to the mm10 transcriptome (Cell Ranger version 1.2). Downstream analyses were performed in R (v.4.0.3) using the Seurat package (v.3.1.1). In the downstream analysis, cells with fewer than 1000 unique genes, greater than 3,500 unique genes, and greater than 6% mitochondrial reads were removed. Genes detected in fewer than three cells across the dataset and cells with fewer than 200 unique genes were also excluded, yielding an expression matrix of 27,362 cells by 14,465 genes.

Gene expression measurements were normalized by total expression per cell and by a scaling factor of 10,000, then transformed using log1p. The top 3,000 most variable features were selected using the vst method in Seurat’s FindVariableFeatures for PCA analysis. The top 15 PCs were calculated and determined to be significant (P < 0.01) using the jackstraw method. A UMAP was calculated from the 15 PCs using default parameters. Unsupervised clustering was performed using the Louvain algorithm. The 0.175 resolution clustering was selected for further analysis. All differential expression analyses were performed using a Wilcoxon rank sum test. Log2 fold changes were then used in a pre-ranked gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). All gene sets from the Hallmarks (50 gene sets), C2 (6,290 gene sets), and C7 (5,219 gene sets) databases from MSigDB were tested for a total of 11,559 gene sets. The pre-ranked GSEA was calculated using the Lightweight Iterative Geneset Enrichment in R (LIGER) tool (v.2.0.1).

Pseudobulk samples were created by aggregating the counts for each gene across all cells in each cluster and genotype using functions from the package Rsc (v.0.0.900), after removing cells which were outliers by median absolute deviation (MAD) and considering only genes with greater than 10 total counts for each pseudobulk, using functions from scater (v.1.18.6) and Matrix.utils (v.0.9.8). DESeq2 (v.1.30.1) was used to normalize the pseudobulk counts matrix and R (v.4.0.3) was used to perform PCA and calculate PC loadings. Visualizations were created with ggplot2 (v.3.3.5) and ComplexHeatmap (v.2.6.2).

CRISPick (broad.io/crispick) was used for off-target analysis of the sgRNAs utilized to generate the enhancer-deleted mouse. Genes with a predicted edit in the coding region (Tier I) and with an off-target cutting frequency determination greater than 0.3 were selected for expression analysis.

### ATAC-seq library preparation and analysis

D3.5 ATAC-seq samples were generated, prepared, sequenced, and analyzed by the Scharer group at Emory University. To generate adequate cell numbers for early recovery, WT C56BL/6J recipient mice were irradiated (400 rad) on D-4. On D0, recipients received 6.0E6 P14+ CD8+ T cells loaded with CellTrace Violet (ThermoFisher) and 2.0E6 splenocytes by intravenous injection prior to infection with LCMV Armstrong or LCMV Clone 13 (as described above). Cells were harvested from the spleen at D3.5 as described above. Cells were sorted (CD8+Thy1.1+Thy1.2−CD62L−CTVloPD-1+), and 10,000 cells per sample were collected. Samples were tagmented with in house-produced Tn5 in TD Buffer (Illumina) for 1 hour at 37C prior to nuclear lysis and DNA purification with SPRI beads (Beckman Coulter)[43]. Samples were then PCR amplified using Nextera Indexing Primers (Illumina) and HiFi HotStart polymerase (KAPA Biosystems) followed by final size selection with SPRI beads and quantification with Illumina qPCR Quant Kit (KAPA Biosystems). Sequencing was performed on a NextSeq550 sequencer using paired-end 75 bp reads. Reads were aligned using bowtie2 (v2.2.4), trimmed using CutAdapt (v2.8), and duplicates were removed with Picard prior to visualization using Integrative Genomics Viewer (v.2.11.0, Broad Institute).

For preparation of D30 ATAC-seq samples, EnhDel and PD-1 KO P14+ cells, or EnhDel and WT P14+ cells, were co-transferred as described above into C57/BL6J recipients. At day 30 after infection with LCMV Clone 13, transferred cells were recovered using the CD8a+ T cell isolation kit (Miltenyi) then stained with CD45.1-PE and enriched with anti-PE microbeads (Miltenyi). After pooling into two biological replicates, 5,000 to 50,000 cells per genotype/subset combination (EnhDel, WT and PD-1 KO; progenitor: Slamf6+ TIM3−, terminal: Slamf6− TIM3+ CX3CR1−) were sorted (FACSAria II Cell Sorter, BD Biosciences) into PBS with 10% FBS.

Pelleted cells were resuspended in 5–50 μl of reaction mix containing 2 × Tagment DNA buffer, Tn5 enzyme, 2% digitonin in nuclease-free water, then incubated at 37°C for 30 min with agitation [44]. MinElute Reaction Cleanup kit (Qiagen) was used for DNA purification. Following PCR, bead cleanup was done using AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter/Agencourt), and library quality was verified using Tapestation analysis. Sequencing was performed on an Illumina NextSeq500 sequencer using paired-end 37 bp reads.

Raw fastq files were merged across lanes. Trimmomatic (v.0.36) was used for quality trimming and primer removal. Trimmed reads were aligned with Bowtie2 (v.2.2.9) to mm10, with a maximum insert size of 1,000 bases. Aligned bams were sorted and duplicates were marked (Picard v.2.8.0). Reads that mapped to the blacklist region were removed. MACS (v.2.1.1) was used to perform peak-calling on merged bam files (Samtools v.1.3.1) from biological replicates using a q value threshold of 0.001. TDF files were generated using igvtools (v.2.3.98) for visualization. Consensus peaks from all samples were merged to create a single peak universe. A raw counts matrix was generated for each biological replicate by quantifying the number of cut sites within each peak region. The Combat-seq method was used to batch-correct samples sequenced at different time points (sva v.3.35.2). Peaks with fewer than 5 reads across all samples were removed. DESeq2 (v.1.30.1) was used for counts matrix normalization and for differential accessibility analysis between each genotype in a one versus one comparison within exhausted subset.

Footprinting analysis was performed on the -23.8 kb Pdcd1 enhancer region. To enhance the signal-to-noise ratio, bam files for WT and PD-1 KO samples were merged using samtools (v1.5). Correction of Tn5 insertion bias, calculation of footprint scores, and estimation of bound/unbound transcription factor binding sites was performed using the ATACorrect, ScoreBigwig, and BINDetect command line tools in the TOBIAS package (v.0.14.0), testing the core set of non-redundant, vertebrate motifs from the JASPAR database (JASPAR2022). Downstream analysis and visualizations were made in R (v.4.0.3).

### Bulk RNA-seq sample preparation and analysis

For preparation of D9 bulk RNA-seq samples, EnhDel and WT P14+ cells were co-transferred as described above into C57/BL6J recipients. At day 9 after infection with LCMV Cl. 13, transferred cells were recovered using the CD8a+ T cell isolation kit (Miltenyi). Cells were sorted by genotype (EnhDel/WT) and subset (progenitor: Slamf6+ TIM3−, terminal: Slamf6− TIM3+ CX3CR1−) and pooled (2 mice per sample) for a recovery of 6,000 to 40,000 cells per sample, as described above for the ATAC-Seq.

RNA isolation and library generation was performed using a modified version of the SmartSeq2 protocol[45, 46]. Cell lysates were thawed on ice. RNA was purified using RNAClean XP beads (Beckman Coulter/Agencourt) prior to resuspension in 4μL of Mix-1 containing primer (IDT) 5′–AAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGTACT30VN-3′, dNTPs (Thermo-Fisher), Recombinant RNase Inhibitor (Takara Bio), and nuclease-free water. Plates were incubated for 3 minutes at 72°C. Reverse transcription was performed by adding 7μL of Mix-2 containing nuclease-free water, 5X Maxima RT buffer (Thermo Scientific), betaine (B0300), MgCl2 (Thermo Scientific), TSO primer (IDT) 5′-AAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGTACATrGrG+G-3′, Recombinant RNase Inhibitor (Takara Bio), and Maxima H Minus Reverse Transcriptase (Thermo Scientific), followed by thermocycler incubation for 90 minutes at 50°C, then 5 minutes at 85°C. PCR preamplification was performed by adding 14μL of Mix-3 containing nuclease-free water, ISPCR primer (IDT) 5′-AAGCAGTGGTATCAACGCAGAGT-3′, and 2X KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix (Roche), followed by whole-transcriptome amplification. Reaction cleanup and primer dimer removal was performed with AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter/Agencourt). cDNA concentration was determined using the Qubit dsDNA high sensitivity assay kit (Thermo Scientific), and cDNA size distribution was evaluated via TapeStation using a High Sensitivity D5000 Screentape (Agilent). The cDNA library was generated using the Nextera XT Library prep kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturer’s protocol using barcodes from the Nextera XT Index Kit v2 Set A (Illumina). Barcoded samples were pooled and cleaned using AMPure XP beads (Beckman Coulter/Agencourt). The pooled library was sequenced on a NextSeq1000 sequencer using paired-end 50-base reads.

Quality of the bulk RNA-seq FASTQ files was determined using FastQC (v0.11.8) and MultiQC (v1.19), and low quality samples were removed (% duplicates > 60, % aligned < 67). FASTQ preprocessing, including adapter sequence and low quality base trimming, was performed using fastp (v0.23.4). Transcript-level quantification of gene expression was then performed using Kallisto (v0.50.1), with the Mus musculus cDNA FASTA (GRCm39) serving as input for generation of the index for pseudoalignment.

A gene level counts matrix was generated by associating transcripts with gene names. Any genes present in only one sample were removed. R (v.4.0.3) was used to perform PCA. DESeq2 (v.1.30.1) was used to normalize the resulting counts matrix and perform differential gene expression analysis between EnhDel and WT prog. samples, and between EnhDel and WT term. samples. As described above, pre-ranked GSEA was calculated using LIGER (v.2.0.1) using a custom set of MSigDB gene sets (all of Hallmarks, Reactome, and subset of T-cell related C7 for a total of 3,036 gene sets). Downstream visualizations were created with ggplot2 (v.3.3.5) and ComplexHeatmap (v.2.6.2).

### Experimental design, sample selection, and statistical analysis

Recipient mice were randomized across cages before starting experiments to minimize cage-to-cage variation. For single transfer experiments, investigators were blinded to transfer genotype. Sample sizes of 5–10 animals per experimental arm per experimental replicate were chosen based on previous studies. Every experiment shown, with the exception of the scRNA-seq and ATAC-seq experiments, and the day 7 single transfer data, is representative of or the combination of two or more experimental replicates, as noted in the legend. All samples shown represent distinct samples.

For LCMV Clone 13 experiments, quality of chronic infection was evaluated by PD-1 expression at day 30. Samples in which the WT term.-exhausted (Slamf6− TIM3+ CX3CR1−) PD-1+ percentage was less than 98% were excluded from all analysis. Additionally, flow cytometry subsets or populations with less than 100 events were excluded from further sub-analysis.

Paired two-sided t-tests were run in Microsoft Excel on comparisons within experimental animals (e.g., co-transfer experiments). Data from EnhDel versus WT animals at baseline, as well as single-transfer experiments, were analyzed using unpaired two-sided Student’s t-tests, also in Microsoft Excel. Prism (v9.0.2, GraphPad) was used for data visualization. Statistical analysis of differential gene expression for the scRNA-seq pseudobulk data and differential chromatin accessibility tests for the bulk ATAC-seq data were done using DESeq2 (v.1.30.1), and FDR correction was performed using the Benjamini-Hochberg method in R (v.4.0.3). P-values and q-values ≤0.05 were considered to indicate a significant difference. Asterisks used to indicate significance correspond to the following: ns, not significant (P> 0.05), *P≤ 0.05, **P≤ 0.01, ***P≤0.001 and ****P≤0.0001. Errors bars shown represent standard deviation, with the exception of numerical advantage ratio (Figure 2C) and weight loss curves (Figure 7B) in which they represent standard error mean.
